items.title: Navigating the Rugged Data Landscape: The Impact of Data-Extrapolation Technologies on Knowledge Production
items.abstract: Data-extrapolation technologies enable progress by importing and applying empirical patterns from one domain to another. Their reliance on empirical patterns, however, is also their limitation: these tools can only be applied where data are abundant. Using the setting of structural biology, I investigate the impact of a data-extrapolation technology on innovation. I exploit the variation in prior data availability to compare areas in which the tool was usable to those in which it was not. I find that the tool increased the quantity of research in data-rich areas: the resulting output yielded limited biological insights but was methodologically rigorous and contributed to downstream research. This paper was accepted by Toby Stuart, entrepreneurship and innovation. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.04115 .

items.title: Dual‐Rule Logical Neural Network for Explainable Credit Scoring
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Credit scoring requires modeling complex nonlinear relationships between borrower characteristics and default risk, yet highly expressive predictive models often suffer from limited transparency and weak generalization on small‐scale financial datasets. To address this challenge, this study proposes an interpretable Dual‐Rule Logical Neural Network (DLNet) for credit risk assessment. DLNet first converts continuous features into explicit binary threshold conditions, and then learns risk patterns through differentiable logical operators that explicitly construct conjunctive and disjunctive rule structures. To further improve rule compactness and readability, an explicit logic‐level sparse regularization term is imposed on the continuous logical weights during training, encouraging concise logical connections without penalizing the final prediction layer. In addition, a local rule backtracking extractor is developed to generate instance‐level explanations by tracing the top‐contributing activated logical nodes back to their corresponding threshold or categorical conditions. Experiments on four real‐world credit datasets show that DLNet achieves competitive predictive performance while providing both global rule patterns and local sample‐specific rationales. The learned rules further reveal heterogeneous logical structures across datasets, with disjunctive, conjunctive, and atomic patterns all appearing among high‐contribution rules. These results demonstrate that DLNet offers a practical framework for combining predictive effectiveness, structural sparsity, and decision transparency in credit scoring.

items.title: Selection into Financial Education and Effects on Portfolio Choice
items.abstract: We study the impact of a financial education program on portfolio choices in a setting that allows us to examine both participation decisions and differences in program benefits across individuals. We directly elicit willingness to pay for financial education and show that individuals with higher financial literacy, greater confidence in applying new knowledge, and higher expected returns are willing to pay more. Using incentivized portfolio allocation tasks, we develop outcome measures tailored to individual risk preferences and show that financial education improves decision quality along these dimensions. The program increases the share of participants who experience an improvement by 20 percentage points, corresponding to average gains of 3.2 percentage points of initial wealth. Individuals with the highest willingness to participate benefit disproportionately from the program, with important implications for the design and evaluation of financial education initiatives. By isolating a specific investment skill in a setting with voluntary participation, our design sheds light on how selection into financial education shapes measured program effects and informs the assessment of broader workplace and public training programs. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: The authors thank the Pension Research Council of Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania, as well as the Retirement and Savings Institute at HEC Montréal, for generous research funding. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08268 .
